title: DID GOD STOP SPEAKING WHEN THE LAST APOSTLE DIED… OR HAVE WE BEEN SILENCING WHAT THE HOLY SPIRIT NEVER STOPPED DOING?
paragraphs: DID GOD STOP SPEAKING WHEN THE LAST APOSTLE DIED… OR HAVE WE BEEN SILENCING WHAT THE HOLY SPIRIT NEVER STOPPED DOING?

Prophecy. Miraculous healing. The gifts of the Holy Spirit. Two thousand years after Pentecost, Christians are still divided over one haunting question: Did these gifts disappear with the apostles, or is the same Spirit who moved through the early Church still working among us today? The answer may challenge what you have been taught, expose what you have been afraid to believe, and bring you face-to-face with the Jesus who never changes.
Imagine this.
You're sitting in a hospital hallway at two in the morning.
The fluorescent lights are painfully bright. Your phone is nearly dead. The coffee in your hand has gone cold.
Behind a closed door is someone you love.
Someone you've been praying for.
Someone the doctors have told you may not survive.
And suddenly, all the theological arguments you've heard about miracles feel terribly personal.
You remember the stories.
Jesus touching lepers.
Blind eyes opening.
A paralyzed man standing up and carrying the mat he had been lying on.
Peter telling a man who had never walked to rise in the name of Jesus Christ.
Paul praying for the sick.
The early Church witnessing things that could not be explained by ordinary human ability.
And then a question rises from somewhere deep inside your exhausted heart.
"Lord… do You still do things like that?"
Not because you want a spectacle.
Not because you're chasing signs.
Not because you believe God owes you a miracle.
But because you love someone.
Because you're afraid.
Because the Bible says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

And because somewhere between your faith and your fear, you're trying to understand whether the gifts described in Scripture were temporary signs for a temporary generation… or expressions of the Holy Spirit's continuing work in Christ's Church.
Perhaps you've been told that prophecy ended when the apostles died.
Perhaps you've been taught that miraculous healing belonged only to the first century.
Or perhaps you grew up in a church where people claimed to prophesy every Sunday, but some of those prophecies left you confused, frightened, manipulated, or spiritually wounded.
Maybe someone once told you that your loved one wasn't healed because you didn't have enough faith.
Maybe someone claimed God had given them a message about your future, and when it never happened, they blamed you instead of questioning their own claim.
And maybe you've quietly wondered whether the real problem is not that Christians disagree about spiritual gifts.
Maybe it's that we've sometimes allowed our disagreements to distract us from the One who gives them.
Because before we ask whether prophecy and healing continue today, we need to remember something that changes the entire conversation.
The Holy Spirit was never given to make human beings impressive. He was given to glorify Jesus Christ.
And any discussion of spiritual gifts that forgets that truth has already lost its way.
The apostle Paul understood this.
When he wrote to the Christians in Corinth, he wasn't addressing a congregation that had everything figured out.
Quite the opposite.
Corinth was a church filled with spiritual activity and serious spiritual problems.
There were divisions.
Pride.
Moral compromise.
Competition.
Confusion about worship.
And believers who seemed more interested in displaying spiritual power than demonstrating Christlike love.
Sound familiar?
Two thousand years have passed, but the human heart hasn't changed nearly as much as we would like to believe.
We still compare ourselves with other believers.
We still mistake visibility for spiritual maturity.
We still sometimes assume that the loudest person in the room must be the most anointed.
And we still struggle to distinguish genuine spiritual fruit from religious performance.
Into that confusion, Paul wrote words that deserve to be heard again.
In 1 Corinthians 12:7, the Greek text reads:
Ἑκάστῳ δὲ δίδοται ἡ φανέρωσις τοῦ πνεύματος πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον.
Hekastō de didotai hē phanerōsis tou pneumatos pros to sympheron.
A faithful translation is:
"To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good."
Notice those final words.
For the common good.
The Greek expression pros to sympheron communicates the idea of what is beneficial or advantageous.
Not for personal celebrity.
Not for spiritual superiority.
Not for building an empire around a preacher's personality.
Not for making vulnerable people dependent on someone who claims special access to God.
The gifts are given for the good of others.
That means a genuine spiritual gift is never a license to abandon humility, accountability, biblical truth, or love.
If someone claims to possess the gift of prophecy but uses it to control people, something is deeply wrong.
If someone claims the gift of healing but exploits the sick for money, something is deeply wrong.
If someone claims to speak for God but refuses to have their words examined by Scripture, something is deeply wrong.
Because the Holy Spirit does not contradict the character of the Christ He glorifies.
And that brings us to the question that has divided faithful Christians for generations.
Did the miraculous gifts end with the apostles?
Some Christians believe they did.
This position is commonly called cessationism.

Cessationists generally believe that certain miraculous or revelatory gifts, particularly prophecy, tongues, and gifts of healing as described in the apostolic era, were given for a foundational period in the Church's history.
They point to passages such as Ephesians 2:20, where Paul describes the Church as built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ Himself as the cornerstone.
Their reasoning deserves serious consideration.
A foundation is laid at the beginning of a building.
It is not laid repeatedly with every new generation.
They also point to Hebrews 2:3–4, where signs, wonders, miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit accompanied the confirmation of the message of salvation.
From this perspective, miraculous gifts served a particular role in authenticating the apostolic witness and establishing the Church.
Many cessationists also emphasize that the completed Scriptures provide the authoritative revelation Christians need for faith and obedience.
These concerns are not automatically evidence of unbelief.
Many cessationists deeply love Jesus, affirm God's sovereignty, believe He can still perform miracles, and faithfully pray for the sick.
They distinguish between God miraculously healing someone today and an individual possessing an ongoing apostolic-era gift of healing.
That distinction matters.
But there is another position held by many equally sincere, Bible-believing Christians.
It is commonly called continuationism.
Continuationists believe that the New Testament does not clearly teach that all miraculous spiritual gifts would cease with the death of the apostles.

They point out that 1 Corinthians 12–14 addresses the functioning of spiritual gifts within the gathered Church, and Paul gives instructions for their proper use rather than announcing an expiration date.
They also appeal to Acts 2, where Peter interprets the events of Pentecost through the prophecy of Joel.
Listen carefully to Acts 2:17–18.
The Greek begins:
Καὶ ἔσται ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις, λέγει ὁ θεός, ἐκχεῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός μου ἐπὶ πᾶσαν σάρκα.
Kai estai en tais eschatais hēmerais, legei ho theos, ekcheō apo tou pneumatos mou epi pasan sarka.
"And it shall be in the last days, God says, that I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh."
Peter continues by describing sons and daughters prophesying, young men seeing visions, old men dreaming dreams, and even male and female servants receiving the Spirit and prophesying.
This is extraordinary.
In the original Hebrew of Joel 2:28, corresponding to Joel 3:1 in some Hebrew versifications, we read:
וְהָיָה אַחֲרֵי־כֵן אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת־רוּחִי עַל־כָּל־בָּשָׂר
Ve-hayah acharei-khen eshpokh et-ruchi al-kol-basar.
"And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh."
The phrase al-kol-basar means "upon all flesh."
In context, this does not mean every individual automatically receives every spiritual gift.
It points to the remarkable breadth of God's promised outpouring, crossing boundaries of age, sex, and social status among those receiving His Spirit.
Peter identifies Pentecost as the fulfillment of Joel's promise, while the broader prophecy also contains language concerning the coming day of the Lord.
Continuationists therefore understand the outpouring of the Spirit as belonging to the era inaugurated by Christ's exaltation and Pentecost, rather than being restricted to the original apostles.
But we must be careful.
Acts 2 does not explicitly settle every question about the duration of each particular gift.
And Ephesians 2:20 does not explicitly state that every miraculous gift ceased when the apostles died.
Both sides make theological arguments from the biblical evidence.
Neither side should pretend that every detail of this debate is answered by one isolated verse.
We honor Scripture best when we refuse to make it say more than it actually says.
And perhaps the passage most frequently discussed in this debate is 1 Corinthians 13.
Paul writes:
At first glance, someone might say, "There it is. Prophecies will end."
And yes, Paul absolutely says they will.
The question is when.
In verse 10, the Greek reads:
ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται.
Hotan de elthē to teleion, to ek merous katargēthēsetai.
"But when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with." (WEB)
The key expression is to teleion.
It refers to what is complete, mature, or perfect, depending on context.
Some have argued that this points to the completion of the New Testament canon.
But the passage itself never explicitly identifies to teleion as the completed Bible.
And the surrounding verses deserve our attention.
Paul says that now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face.
Now he knows in part, but then he will know fully, even as he has been fully known.
Many interpreters understand this language as pointing toward the fullness of knowledge and communion associated with Christ's return and the consummation of God's kingdom.
That interpretation provides a significant argument for continuationism.
Still, Christians differ over the precise relationship between Paul's teaching here and the duration of particular gifts.
What cannot be missed is Paul's central message.
Love is greater than every gift.
Greater than prophecy.
Greater than tongues.
Greater than extraordinary knowledge.
Greater than the ability to astonish a congregation.
You can speak eloquently about the supernatural and still be cruel to your family.
You can debate spiritual gifts for hours and refuse to forgive someone who hurt you.
You can defend the doctrine of divine healing while showing no compassion toward a person suffering through chemotherapy.
You can be so determined to prove your theology correct that you forget the wounded human being sitting across from you.
And Paul says that without love, even the most extraordinary spiritual activity amounts to nothing.
Think about that.
A church can be loud and spiritually immature.
A church can be quiet and spiritually alive.
A church can claim miracles and lack integrity.
A church can reject sensationalism and still fail to care for suffering people.
The real question is not simply whether extraordinary gifts are present.
It is whether the people claiming to follow Jesus are becoming more like Jesus.
But what about healing?
Does God still heal?
Here, we need to distinguish two questions that are often confused.
Does God have the power to heal miraculously today?
And does the New Testament gift of healing continue to operate through particular believers today?
Those are related questions, but they are not identical.
Christians across the cessationist and continuationist spectrum commonly affirm that God can heal in response to prayer.
James 5:14–15 instructs the sick to call for the elders of the church, who are to pray over them in the name of the Lord.
The passage does not tell Christians to stop praying for the sick after the apostolic age.
Nor does it authorize us to promise that every sick person will experience immediate physical healing.
And that distinction may be the most important thing someone reading this needs to hear.
Because somewhere right now, a mother is praying over a child who has not recovered.
A husband is holding the hand of a wife whose cancer has returned.
A young believer is trying to understand why the pain hasn't stopped.
And someone has told them, perhaps with terrible confidence, that their suffering proves they don't have enough faith.
Please hear this.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
Your illness is not automatic evidence of hidden sin.
Your need for medication does not make you a second-class Christian.
Seeking qualified medical care is not a betrayal of faith.
And no preacher has the authority to guarantee your healing by a particular date or demand payment as the price of God's mercy.
Remember the apostle Paul.
The same man through whom extraordinary miracles occurred also pleaded with the Lord concerning a thorn in his flesh.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, the Lord answered him:
"My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." (WEB)
We should not assume that Paul's thorn was necessarily a physical illness; Scripture does not settle its precise nature.
But the lesson is unmistakable.
God did not grant Paul's repeated request for its removal.
Instead, He promised sustaining grace.
Paul also wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).
And he instructed Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23).
These passages should make us very cautious about claiming that faithful Christians will always be healed if they simply believe strongly enough.
Even in the apostolic age, the biblical record does not portray every illness as instantly removed.
That does not mean we should stop praying boldly.
It means we should pray boldly without pretending to control the outcome.
We can ask God for a miracle.
We can seek medical treatment.
We can trust His goodness.
We can grieve when healing does not come.
And we can refuse to turn someone's suffering into a verdict against their faith.
There is something profoundly beautiful about a church that prays for healing and continues loving the sick person even when no miracle occurs.
A church that brings meals.
Pays a hospital bill when it can.
Sits through another long night.
Listens without offering shallow explanations.
And refuses to disappear when the testimony doesn't end the way everyone hoped.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing in the room is not a dramatic declaration.
Sometimes it is a believer quietly remaining beside someone who is hurting.
Now consider prophecy.
The Greek noun commonly translated "prophecy" is προφητεία — prophēteia.
In the New Testament, prophecy involves communication presented as arising from divine revelation or inspiration.
But we must not reduce the entire subject to predicting future events.
In 1 Corinthians 14:3, Paul writes:
Edification.
Exhortation.
Consolation.
The Greek terms point toward building up, encouragement or appeal, and comfort.
This matters because prophecy in Corinth was being evaluated partly by its effect upon the gathered Church.
Yet Paul does not permit believers to accept every claimed prophecy without examination.
In 1 Corinthians 14:29, he instructs that two or three prophets should speak and the others should discern or evaluate.
The Greek verb διακρινέτωσαν — diakrinetōsan conveys the idea of discerning or weighing what has been said.
And in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21, Paul writes:
Notice the balance.
Do not despise.
But test.
Do not automatically reject.
But do not automatically believe.
The New Testament does not commend gullibility as a spiritual virtue.
A person saying "God told me" does not exempt that person from examination.
No modern prophecy has the authority to overturn Scripture.
No claimed revelation can replace the Gospel.
No supposed word from God should be used to pressure someone into an abusive relationship, surrender financial control, abandon necessary treatment, or obey a leader without question.
And Christians disagree about whether contemporary prophecy, if it occurs, should be understood in the same way as biblical prophetic revelation.
That is an important theological question, not a minor technicality.
What Christians can agree on is that the prophetic Scriptures remain authoritative, Jesus Christ is the definitive revelation of God, and every spiritual claim must be tested against biblical truth.
Hebrews 1:1–2 reminds us that God, who formerly spoke through the prophets, has spoken to us in His Son.
That means Jesus is not merely one voice among many.
He is the center of God's saving revelation.
The measure of spiritual maturity is not how many private revelations a person claims to receive.
It is whether that person listens to Christ, believes His Word, and obeys Him.
And perhaps this is where the debate becomes painfully personal.
Because some believers have become so afraid of deception that they are afraid even to ask God to work powerfully.
Others have become so hungry for supernatural experiences that they barely open their Bibles anymore.
One group may be tempted to treat every unusual testimony with suspicion.
Another may be tempted to treat every emotional experience as divine revelation.
But Scripture calls us to something better than either fear or credulity.
It calls us to truth.
Humility.
Discernment.
Love.
And wholehearted devotion to Jesus.
In 1 Corinthians 12:11, Paul explains that the one and same Spirit works these gifts, distributing to each person individually as He wills.
The Greek phrase καθὼς βούλεται — kathōs bouletai means "as He wills."
Those three words confront every attempt to manufacture spiritual power.
The Spirit distributes as He wills.
Not as a preacher commands.
Not as a church program schedules.
Not as a financial donor purchases.
Not as a believer's desperation demands.
The Holy Spirit is God.
He is not a technique.
He is not a religious product.
He is not an atmosphere that can be artificially manufactured through music, lighting, or emotional pressure.
And He cannot be bought.
Remember Simon in Acts 8?
When Simon saw the Holy Spirit being given through the apostles' laying on of hands, he offered money in an attempt to obtain that power.
Peter rebuked him sharply.
The lesson remains urgent today.
The power of God is not for sale.
And that truth must shape the way Christian ministries handle money, miracles, and spiritual authority.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not a transaction.
Jesus Christ paid the price of our redemption with His own blood.
And that brings us to something even more extraordinary than the debate over miraculous gifts.
The greatest miracle any sinner can receive is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Dragged into public shame.
Surrounded by accusers.
Her sin exposed.
Her future hanging in the balance.
The scene is full of scandal.
And Jesus does not pretend that sin is harmless.
But neither does He join the crowd in treating the woman as disposable.
When her accusers depart, Jesus tells her that He does not condemn her and commands her to leave her life of sin.
Mercy does not erase the call to repentance.
Grace does not celebrate what destroys us.
Jesus offers something greater than public humiliation or cheap permission to continue in sin.
He calls sinners into a new life.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
And it is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because our sins were imaginary.
Not because the consequences of our choices never mattered.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored or every earthly wound immediately disappears.
But because Jesus Christ entered our fallen world, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again in victory.
He offers forgiveness to the repentant.
He gives new life to those who trust Him.
He brings people who were far from God near through His blood.
And He begins transforming hearts that could never rescue themselves.
A person can experience a remarkable physical healing and still need salvation.
A person can speak about prophecy and still need repentance.
A person can witness something astonishing and still refuse to surrender to Jesus.
Remember the ten lepers in Luke 17?
All ten were cleansed.
But only one returned to glorify God and thank Jesus.
The miracle mattered.
But the response to the Miracle Worker mattered too.
And that raises a question more searching than whether we have ever witnessed a supernatural healing.
If God answered every prayer you prayed for physical relief, but you never truly surrendered your heart to Jesus, what would you have gained for eternity?
That question should humble all of us.
Because we can spend our lives searching for the gifts and overlook the Giver.
We can become fascinated with prophecy while ignoring the clear commands of Scripture.
We can desperately want God to change our circumstances while resisting His work of changing our character.
We can ask Him to remove our pain while refusing to release our bitterness.
We can pray for a miracle in our body while hiding a war inside our soul.
And still, Jesus calls.
Not with a promise that following Him will make every earthly problem disappear.
But with the promise of Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
His presence.
His grace.
His resurrection life.
And a future in which death itself will finally be defeated.
Revelation 21:4 points toward that glorious day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is the Christian's ultimate hope.
Not that every disease will be cured before we die.
But that because Jesus rose from the dead, suffering and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
And perhaps this is where both sides of the spiritual-gifts debate need to examine their hearts.
To the believer who thinks the gifts have ceased:
Do not confuse theological caution with permission to stop expecting God to answer prayer.
The Lord is still sovereign.
He still hears His children.
He still works in ways beyond our understanding.
And even if you believe certain apostolic gifts have fulfilled their foundational purpose, you can pray with confidence that nothing is impossible for God.
To the believer who believes the gifts continue:
Do not confuse spiritual excitement with spiritual maturity.
Do not measure God's presence by noise, emotion, unusual experiences, or dramatic testimonies.
Do not accept every claim of prophecy.
Do not shame the sick.
Do not elevate any gifted personality above the authority of Scripture.
And never forget that the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23 matters profoundly.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
These are not consolation prizes for Christians who have never witnessed a miracle.
They are evidence of the Spirit's transforming work.
A person who claims extraordinary gifts but habitually lacks love, integrity, and self-control has given us serious reason for concern.
And a believer who quietly serves the poor, forgives enemies, remains faithful through suffering, and points others to Christ should never be dismissed as spiritually inferior.
Paul's picture of the Church in 1 Corinthians 12 is not a stage filled with religious celebrities.
It is a body.
Different members.
Different functions.
Mutual dependence.
Shared suffering.
Shared honor.
One Lord.
One Spirit.
One body.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:40, Paul concludes his instructions about gathered worship by saying:
"Let all things be done decently and in order." (WEB)
That is not a command to extinguish spiritual life.
It is a command to conduct worship in a way consistent with God's character and the good of His people.
So, did prophecy and healing end with the apostles?
The most responsible answer is that faithful Christians disagree, and the New Testament does not provide an uncontested, explicit statement that settles every aspect of the question.
Cessationists argue that certain gifts belonged to the foundational apostolic era.
Continuationists argue that Scripture gives no clear termination date for those gifts before Christ's return.
Both positions must be examined through careful interpretation of the whole Bible, not merely through isolated experiences, personal preferences, or inherited traditions.
We should neither invent certainty where Scripture leaves room for debate nor surrender the truths Scripture makes clear.
God is sovereign.
The Holy Spirit is active in Christ's people.
The Church is commanded to pray.
Spiritual claims must be tested.
Love must govern the exercise of every gift.
The Gospel must remain central.
And Jesus Christ alone is worthy of our worship.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent years trapped between two fears.
Afraid of being deceived if you believe God may still work through extraordinary gifts.
Afraid of missing something from God if you question what someone claims is supernatural.
You do not have to live enslaved to either fear.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Seek wisdom.
Learn from faithful believers who disagree with you.
Examine claims carefully.
Refuse manipulation.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
If you believe God may still grant prophecy or gifts of healing, pursue biblical discernment rather than sensationalism.
If you believe certain gifts have ceased, continue praying boldly and trusting God's sovereign power.
And wherever you stand, remember Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 14:1:
"Follow after love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy." (WEB)
Christians differ over how that instruction applies to the Church today, but no Christian has permission to disregard its opening command.
Follow after love.
Because one day, every argument about spiritual gifts will be overshadowed by the glory of the risen Christ.
One day, believers will no longer need to pray over hospital beds.
One day, the redeemed will no longer struggle with the weakness of fallen bodies.
One day, faith will give way to sight.
And the people of God will behold the Savior who was crucified and raised for them.
Until then, we pray.
We study.
We discern.
We serve.
We suffer with those who suffer.
We rejoice with those who rejoice.
And we proclaim Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Not ourselves.
Not our favorite preacher.
Not our preferred theological camp.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
And if this message has challenged something you've believed for years, I want to invite you into a conversation that is more meaningful than an argument.
You don't have to pretend certainty where you still have questions.
Perhaps you've experienced what you believe was a miraculous answer to prayer.
Perhaps you've been wounded by a false prophecy.
Perhaps you've prayed for healing and are still waiting.
Perhaps you've watched someone you love die despite the prayers of an entire church.
Your story matters.
Not because commenting earns God's attention.
Not because a public declaration makes your faith more legitimate.
But because sometimes a struggling believer needs to know they are not struggling alone.
And please, when someone shares a painful testimony, don't rush to correct them with a theological slogan.
Listen.
Pray.
Respond with compassion.
We are not here to win arguments at the expense of wounded souls.
We are here to point one another toward Christ.
Return to 1 Corinthians 12–14, Acts 2, James 5, and the other passages we've explored. Read them slowly. Examine the context. Let God's Word shape your convictions.
That simple act can help carry a Scripture-centered conversation beyond the people our page currently reaches.
Someone may have stopped attending church after being manipulated by a supposed prophet.
Someone may be sitting in a hospital room tonight, wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Someone may have never heard the Gospel explained with both conviction and compassion.
We want believers to grow deeper, seekers to discover the truth of the Gospel, and those who have wandered to hear again the Savior's call to repentance and faith.
Our desire is to help make biblical learning, spiritual nourishment, and practical discipleship resources accessible to people who genuinely want to grow closer to Jesus.
And there is another way you can become part of this mission.
It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter Scripture-centered teaching, Gospel encouragement, and resources for Christian growth.

For those who already practice regular Christian giving, monthly ministry support may be one expression of generosity and an offering toward Gospel work. Scripture teaches the value of supporting faithful ministry, including in Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14.
We want your generosity to come from conviction and love, never pressure or guilt.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, worship, generosity, and faithful service wherever He has placed you.

It can help us devote more time and resources to creating biblical articles, strengthening discipleship materials, maintaining free Christian resources, and expanding the reach of Gospel-centered content.
The greatest gift we can ever point you toward remains freely offered through Jesus Christ.
Because the goal has never been to build a platform bigger than the message.
The goal is to make the message of Jesus Christ known.
And before you leave, I want to bring you back to that hospital hallway.
The cold coffee.
The exhausted prayers.
The closed door.
The trembling question.
"Lord… do You still do things like that?"
Maybe the person you love recovers.
Maybe the doctors witness an improvement they never expected.
Maybe healing comes slowly through treatment, care, and time.
Or maybe, in a way that breaks your heart, the answer you longed for does not come in this life.
I cannot promise you which story will be yours.
No faithful preacher can.
But I can point you to the Savior who stood outside Lazarus's tomb and wept.
The One who did not treat grief as an embarrassment.
The One who entered our suffering.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One whom death could not hold.
The One who promises resurrection life to those who belong to Him.
The Christian hope is not that every prayer ends with the miracle we requested.
It is that Jesus Christ has conquered the grave.
And whether the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit continue in precisely the same ways today remains a matter Christians must study with humility, the Gospel itself is not uncertain.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
And He calls sinners everywhere to repent and believe.
So don't spend your entire life trying to prove that God can perform miracles while refusing the mercy He has already revealed in His Son.
Don't become so fascinated with the possibility of prophecy that you neglect the written Word that points you to Christ.
Don't become so wounded by religious counterfeits that you turn away from the true Shepherd.
And don't become so afraid of suffering that you forget the Savior who has promised never to forsake His people.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him your doubts.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your sins.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the deepest need of the human soul is not to witness something extraordinary.
It is to be reconciled to the living God.
And when the miracle you begged for never comes, may you discover that the crucified and risen Jesus is still worthy of your trust—and that His grace has not let go of you.
